title: Block close: the great conversation
hook: two thousand years of thinkers arguing, praying and adding

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Polkinghorne and the kettle: how it boils, and why. Your line was two windows. Which window did you forget to look through? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-six.

A long table, and the chairs keep filling. At one end, Justin, a teacher in Rome, says the seeds of the Word were scattered everywhere, even among the philosophers. Further down, Augustine is confessing to God out loud. Boethius is talking to Philosophy in his cell. Anselm is trying to think the greatest thing that can be thought. Julian of Norwich, quietly: all shall be well. Luther bangs the table about grace. Pascal mutters about reasons of the heart. Kierkegaard insists on the single person. Bonhoeffer writes questions from prison. And at the near end, the newest arrivals: a priest-physicist, a teacher from the rice fields, a scholar from Kenya. Nobody at this table agrees about everything. Today we close the block of great thinkers by stepping back to see the whole table.
screen: `STEP BACK AND SEE THE WHOLE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Some people call it the great conversation, and it has run for centuries. Here are four things the block showed about it. First, they argued. Anselm built an argument; others pushed back. Aquinas set out his five ways; Ockham shaved away what he thought wasn't needed. Luther and the Catholic thinkers who answered him disagreed deeply. The conversation is honest about that: these thinkers did not speak with one voice. Second, they prayed. These weren't only minds on paper. Augustine wrote his Confessions as a long prayer to God. Dionysius climbed a ladder of names into silence. Simone Weil said attention, at its highest, is prayer. For several of them, thinking about God and talking to God were one act. Third, they added. Nobody started from zero. They picked up what came before and carried it a step. Newman said doctrine grows, like a seed into a tree. Ware handed on the Orthodox way. Mbiti and Koyama asked what the gospel sounds like in their own soil. The letter to the Hebrews pictures the faithful of the past as a crowd in the stands: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight." Fourth, they never finished. The preacher in Ecclesiastes warned, a little wearily: "of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh." Books kept coming anyway, and so did the conversation. That's the good news of an unfinished table: there's still a chair. Anyone who reads, asks, doubts, prays, or writes in a margin is already taking part.

Here's the practice: pick one thinker to read more. Settle, and breathe. Let the faces of this block pass by, one at a time: Augustine, Boethius, Julian, Aquinas, Luther, Pascal, Wesley, Kierkegaard, Bonhoeffer, Weil, Merton, Ware, Koyama, Mbiti, Polkinghorne, and the rest. Don't choose the one you think you should. Notice the one you keep returning to, the one whose question is also yours. Let that one take a seat beside you. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If you don't, just hold their question for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Block close. The end of the great thinkers: people who argued, prayed and added, around a table that still has room.
Your line: join the conversation. Today, find one page by the thinker you chose, even a single paragraph, and read it slowly, pencil in hand. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Christians read the great thinkers of their tradition in study groups, seminaries and on their own, often keeping a favorite writer for years.
